usamts-2015-r2-01.prompt:
In the $6\times 8$ grid below (rows listed from top to bottom, blank squares shown as $\cdot$), the shortest path through unit squares between the pair of 2's has length 2.

$$\begin{array}{|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|c|}\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&6&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&10&1&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&2&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&8\\\hline \cdot&5&\cdot&\cdot&2&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&7&9&\cdot\\\hline \cdot&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot&3&\cdot&\cdot&\cdot\\\hline\end{array}$$

Fill in some of the unit squares in the grid so that

(i) exactly half of the squares in each row and column contain a number,

(ii) each of the numbers 1 through 12 appears exactly twice, and

(iii) for $n = 1, 2, \ldots, 12$, the shortest path between the pair of $n$'s has length exactly $n$.

You do not need to prove that your answer is the only one possible; you merely need to find an answer that satisfies the constraints above.

usamts-2015-r2-02.prompt:
A net for a polyhedron is cut along an edge to give two pieces. For example, we may cut a cube net along the red edge to form two pieces as shown.

Are there two distinct polyhedra for which this process may result in the same two pairs of pieces? If you think the answer is no, prove that no pair of polyhedra can result in the same two pairs of pieces. If you think the answer is yes, prove an example; a clear example will suffice as proof.
usamts-2015-r2-02.answer: Yes. For example, glue a square pyramid with all edges equal to the cube edge onto two **opposite** faces of a cube, or onto two **adjacent** faces. Both polyhedra have nets that, cut along one edge, give the same two pieces: each piece is a domino of two squares with the four triangles of one pyramid attached, as a fan, to a long side of one of the two squares.

usamts-2015-r2-03.prompt:
For all positive integers $n$, show that
$$\frac{1}{n}\sum_{k=1}^{n} \frac{k\cdot k!\cdot\binom{n}{k}}{n^k} = 1.$$
usamts-2015-r2-03.answer: Proof: the sum of the last $r+1$ terms equals $\dfrac{n!}{r!\,n^{n-r-1}}$ (induction on $r$), so the full sum is $n$. Alternatively, the terms divided by $n$ are the probabilities that the first repeat in rolls of an $n$-sided die happens on roll $k+1$.

usamts-2015-r2-04.prompt: Find all polynomials $P(x)$ with integer coefficients such that, for all integers $a$ and $b$, $P(a+b) - P(b)$ is a multiple of $P(a)$.
usamts-2015-r2-04.answer: $P(x) = c$ or $P(x) = cx$, where $c$ is any integer.

usamts-2015-r2-05.prompt:
Let $n > 1$ be an even positive integer. A $2n \times 2n$ grid of unit squares is given, and it is partitioned into $n^2$ contiguous $2 \times 2$ blocks of unit squares. A subset $S$ of the unit squares satisfies the following properties:

(i) For any pair of squares $A$, $B$ in $S$, there is a sequence of squares in $S$ that starts with $A$, ends with $B$, and has any two consecutive elements sharing a side; and

(ii) In each of the $2 \times 2$ blocks of squares, at least one of the four squares is in $S$.

An example for $n = 2$ is shown, with the squares of $S$ shaded and the four $2\times 2$ blocks of squares outlined in bold.

In terms of $n$, what is the minimum possible number of elements in $S$?
